# Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta (DN 22 (PTS DN ii 290))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta ("The Longer Discourse on Mindfulness Meditation", DN 22) is the twenty-second discourse of the Dīghanikāya [SuttaCentral]. Addressed to the monks, it sets forth the practice of mindfulness meditation (satipaṭṭhāna) as the direct path (ekāyano maggo) for the purification of beings, the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, and the realization of Nibbāna [SuttaCentral; Chakma 2015; Anālayo 2006; Crosby 2014]. The discourse consists of two primary divisions: the first provides detailed contemplation instructions covering body, feelings, mind, and dhammas—virtually identical in wording to the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (MN 10)—while the second delivers an elaborate, term-by-term analysis of the four noble truths [Norman 1983; Shonin et al. 2015; Anālayo 2006].
The commentary attributed to Buddhaghosa and the discourse itself have exerted immense influence on Theravāda practice, particularly within Burmese and Shan meditation traditions and modern vipassanā movements, while also functioning as a prominent chanted text and vernacular literary source [Crosby 2014; Khur-Yearn 2012; Anālayo 2018].
Curated parallels include MN 10, the Kāyagatāsati Sutta (MN 119), the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta (MN 141), Chinese Āgama versions in the Madhyamāgama (MĀ 98, MĀ 81, MĀ 31) and Ekottarika Āgama (EĀ 12.1, EĀ 27.1), T 32, and Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 11) [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983]. Its four-truths section is shared with MN 141 and the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga (Vb 4) [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Anālayo, Dawn of Abhidharma]. DharmaNexus confirms massive Pali-internal text reuse with MN 10 (over 231,000 matching characters across §0.2–17.3), the Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga (Vb 7), Saccavibhaṅga (Vb 4), and Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta (SN 47), while aligning it cross-linguistically with the Chinese Madhyamāgama (T 26), Śāntideva's Śikṣāsamuccaya, and the Dharmaskandha [DharmaNexus].
